holidays.name: National Pistachio Day
holidays.description: A day to crack open a bag of the green, crunchy nut and snack away, whether in ice cream, baklava, or straight from the shell.
holidays.origin: Observed in the United States as a food holiday with no single known founder, it grew in popularity through snack marketing and social media as a celebration of the pistachio.
holidays.funFact: Pistachios are technically seeds of a fruit, and their shells split open naturally when the nut is ripe. Growers call this the nut 'smiling'.

holidays.name: Tell a Fairy Tale Day
holidays.description: A day for gathering friends or family and sharing a fairy tale, whether a classic about dragons and princesses or one you invent on the spot.
holidays.origin: It is an unofficial observance meant to encourage storytelling and the oral tradition, and it is often tied to libraries, schools, and storytelling groups.
holidays.funFact: Many fairy tales, such as the ones collected by the Brothers Grimm, were much darker in their earliest versions and were not originally meant for children.

holidays.name: For Whom the Cowbell Tolls Day
holidays.description: A day to celebrate the cowbell, the percussion instrument made famous by a classic Saturday Night Live sketch in which someone always needs more of it.
holidays.origin: The date nods to the cowbell sketch 'More Cowbell,' featuring Will Ferrell and Christopher Walken, with the holiday name playing on the title For Whom the Bell Tolls.
holidays.funFact: The sketch spoofed the recording of Blue Öyster Cult's '(Don't Fear) The Reaper,' which really does feature a cowbell, played by producer Bruce Botnick.

holidays.name: Carnation Day
holidays.description: A day for wearing or gifting carnations, one of the oldest cultivated flowers, in honor of its ruffled petals and long symbolic history.
holidays.origin: The day is tied to the flower's role in tributes and remembrance, notably in Ohio, where the carnation is the state flower in honor of President William McKinley, who often wore one.
holidays.funFact: Carnations can come in many colors, and in the 1970s Portugal's Carnation Revolution made the flower a symbol of peaceful political change.
